text_to_speech: Protein is sort of a basic structure that's found in all of life. It's a molecule. And so I like to visualize this with a kind of bracelet analogy. This is from my son, but these beads represent kind of individual amino acids. So protein, essentially is a string that's made up of these little individual pieces. And there's 20 different amino acids that you can combine and in any kind of different way. The last thing is a protein doesn't usually exist as a string, but actually folds up into a particular shape, depending on the order and how those different amino acids interact together. Amino acids in our body come from the food that we eat. And we also make them so you know, other animals make proteins. So we eat those, take those in, and we actually, take that chain and break it down into the individual amino acids. And then we can rebuild it any kind of combination that we want. So it turns out, we can make about half of our amino acids on our own, but the other half we have to get from our food. So meat, and things like that have a lot of protein content in them. and a lot has to do with muscle, a lot of protein is required to make your muscles, muscles move. And then once they're broken down, they kind of float around in the inside the cell, those little individual beads in our analogy. And then inside the cell, your body basically connects them together to make the proteins that your body needs to make. And then in our own body, you know, it's still kind of debated how many different kinds of proteins but there's also there's lots of different ways in which we combine these little bead like amino acids into longer chains. So yeah, proteins carry out a lot of different roles in the cell. There's kind of a few different main categories they fall into. One is structural, right, so your body is made up of particular structures, and it can be kind of string like structures or globules or things that can anchor from one cell to another, and so proteins take on that role. Another big role that they take on is kind of biochemistry. How your body carries out particular reactions in your cell from breaking down fat or amino acids, or other proteins that we talked about to carry on oxygen, right? Hemoglobin is an example of a protein. So they're carrying out these special chemical reactions inside yourself. And there's, you know, a number of other reactions that happen, but those are kind of two main categories of functions that your protein proteins carry out in the cell.

youtube_description:
Nathan Ahlgren is a professor of biology at Clark University. In this interview, he explains exactly what a protein is, how they are made, and the wide variety of functions they perform in our body.

The full article is available to read at The Conversation US: https://theconversation.com/what-is-a-protein-a-biologist-explains-152870
